passage: At the village tea stall, Tushar took his tea, looked at Ganga's new haircut without any expression, and said, "Very bold. Did the buffalo help?" Nobody laughed. Ganga's hand went to her hair. His face was as flat as a slate, and the tea seller stopped stirring. Tushar sipped and waited. Ganga couldn't tell whether he meant it kindly or cruelly. Three weeks ago she wouldn't have hesitated, because they had known each other forever, but he'd been teasing everyone lately. "Tushar, are you joking?" she asked. A tiny twitch appeared at the corner of his mouth. "Obviously. It looks good. I'm just bad at compliments." She let out her breath and laughed.

qa.q: What did Tushar ask about Ganga's haircut?
qa.a: He asked, 'Did the buffalo help?'

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking when Tushar said it without any expression?
qa.a: She was unsure whether it was a joke or an insult; the flat face gave her nothing to go on, and she felt worried about her hair.

qa.q: What could Tushar do so his deadpan jokes don't hurt?
qa.a: He could add a small signal like a smile or check that the other person is in on it, especially when they can't tell.

qa.q: How might the tea seller have read the moment?
qa.a: The tea seller stopped stirring, so they may have been unsure too, since deadpan needs shared understanding and an onlooker doesn't have it.

grounding: A teen delivers a joke or insult with no expression, listeners can't tell if it's humour, and asking settles it.

passage: In the school canteen in Addis Ababa, Yara finished her class presentation and sat down with her lunch, still shaky. Abebe leaned over the table, face perfectly still, and said, "Your presentation was the longest ten minutes of my life." Yara froze with her fork in the air. His eyes gave nothing away. Other boys at the next table looked up. She felt her cheeks heat, because she had worked hard on it. Then she remembered how he talked to his brother, the same dry voice. "Is that a joke, Abebe, or do you mean it?" He blinked. "A joke. I couldn't stop watching. I'm sorry, I should smile when I do that." Yara laughed a little unsteadily.

qa.q: Where were Abebe and Yara when he spoke?
qa.a: They were in the school canteen in Addis Ababa.

qa.q: What might Yara be feeling when Abebe says her presentation was the longest ten minutes of his life?
qa.a: She might feel hurt and embarrassed, since she worked hard and his face showed nothing, but she is also unsure whether it was a joke.

qa.q: What could Abebe do differently next time?
qa.a: He could add a smile or a warm word to show he is joking, or say it in private, since his deadpan style needs shared understanding.

qa.q: How might the boys at the next table see the exchange?
qa.a: They may see a joke or an insult, depending on what they know of Abebe, and they don't have Yara's history with his dry voice.

grounding: A teen's deadpan joke lands as possible insult, and asking settles it, since deadpan needs shared understanding.

passage:
In the school canteen, Saurabh put down Aparna's poem after reading it, looked at her with a completely blank face, and said, "That is the worst thing I've ever read. I'm going to need therapy."
Aparna's stomach dropped. She'd spent two weeks on it.
Saurabh took a bite of his paratha. His face didn't move at all.
She couldn't tell. His voice was flat. His eyes gave nothing away. Was this one of his jokes? He did this all the time with his brother. But she'd only known him since June.
"Are you joking?" she asked. "Because I can't tell, and I actually care about this one."
He blinked, then his face cracked into a grin. "Joking! It's brilliant. The line about the ceiling fan got me. Sorry, I forget people don't know my face yet."
Aparna let out a breath and laughed. "Next time, joke after the compliment."
"Deal."

qa.q: How long had Aparna spent on the poem?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling after Saurabh's deadpan remark?
qa.a: Aparna felt hurt and anxious, her stomach dropping, unsure whether he was joking about something she cared about.

qa.q: Which choice of Aparna's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking "Are you joking?" worked, because Saurabh's flat face gave no clues and they hadn't known each other long enough to share his humour.

qa.q: How did Saurabh see his own remark?
qa.a: He saw it as an obvious joke, like the ones he made with his brother, forgetting that newer friends couldn't read his blank face yet.

grounding: The scene shows a deadpan joke being unclear to someone without shared understanding, and asking settling it.

passage:
Hi Joseph,
Quick question, and I hope this doesn't sound weird.
When I told you on the exchange group call that I'd won the state photography award, you said, with a totally straight face, "Great. Another award. How tragic for you." Then you looked at the camera and didn't smile.
Everyone else laughed, so I laughed too. But afterwards I kept replaying it. I honestly couldn't tell if it was a joke, or if you were annoyed that I talk about photography too much.
I know people from your town are supposed to have very dry humour. My cousin in Leeds does the same thing. But we've only known each other three weeks, and I can't read you yet.
So: were you joking? If yes, great, I'll learn. If no, tell me, and I'll talk less about photos.
Raghav

qa.q: How long have Raghav and Joseph known each other?
qa.a: Three weeks.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling after the group call?
qa.a: Raghav felt unsure and uneasy, replaying Joseph's deadpan comment and worrying Joseph was annoyed.

qa.q: What makes Raghav's email a good way to handle the uncertainty?
qa.a: It asks directly and kindly whether it was a joke, without accusing, and offers to adjust either way.

qa.q: How might Joseph have seen that comment?
qa.a: Joseph probably meant it as friendly dry humour and may be surprised it caused doubt.

grounding: The email shows a teenager unable to tell whether a deadpan remark was humour and settling it by asking.

passage:
So, I'm Asif, and my whole family talks in deadpan. My sister will say, "Wow, your cooking has improved, it's only slightly poisonous," and we all laugh. It's how we show love.
When Sunaina joined our class, I did the same. She showed me her new cycle, and I said, very seriously, "That is the ugliest cycle in Hyderabad. I'm calling the police."
She just looked at me. Didn't laugh. Went quiet the rest of the day.
I didn't get it. At home that would be a compliment.
Next day she asked me, "Were you making fun of my cycle? My father saved for months for it."
I felt terrible. I said, "No! I love it. That's just how I joke. I should have smiled."
She said, "Maybe just tell me when you're joking, until I learn your face."
Now I smile after. Or I just say the nice thing.

qa.q: What did Asif say about Sunaina's cycle?
qa.a: "That is the ugliest cycle in Hyderabad. I'm calling the police."

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling after the joke?
qa.a: Sunaina felt hurt and unsure, going quiet, especially because her father had saved for months for the cycle.

qa.q: What did Sunaina and Asif agree on?
qa.a: That Asif would show or say when a joke was a joke, until Sunaina learned Asif's deadpan style.

qa.q: How does Asif's family see deadpan humour?
qa.a: For Asif's family, deadpan insults are a shared joke and a way of showing love.

grounding: The spoken account shows deadpan humour needing shared understanding, and a listener asking to settle whether it was a joke.

passage: I sit behind Saurabh in maths, so I've had two years of his face, which never moves. On Monday Kashish came in with a new short haircut, and Saurabh looked at her for a long second and said, completely flat, "Bold. Very brave choice." No smile. No eyebrow. Nothing. Half the row laughed, because with Saurabh that's usually a joke. Kashish didn't. She touched the back of her neck and sat down slowly. From where I sat, I honestly couldn't tell if he meant it as a compliment, a joke or a dig. I don't think Kashish could either. At break she turned round and asked him straight: "Was that a joke or a dig? I really can't tell with you." Saurabh blinked. For the first time in two years I saw his face do something; it looked worried. "Joke. Compliment joke. It looks good. Sorry, I forget people can't read me." Kashish nodded. "Maybe smile next time."

qa.q: What did Saurabh say about the haircut?
qa.a: He said, completely flat, "Bold. Very brave choice."

qa.q: What might Kashish have been feeling when she touched the back of her neck?
qa.a: Kashish may have felt self-conscious and a little hurt, unsure whether the flat comment was a dig at the new haircut; it could also have been simple confusion.

qa.q: Why was Kashish's direct question a good move?
qa.a: Deadpan gives no cues, so asking 'Was that a joke or a dig?' settled it quickly and let Saurabh explain it was a compliment.

qa.q: How did Saurabh see his own comment?
qa.a: Saurabh meant it as a joking compliment and was worried to realise people can't read his flat face.

grounding: It shows a deadpan remark that listeners cannot read as joke or insult, seen by an observer, and a direct question settling it.
